scenes.head: The balance sheet and equity
scenes.sub: Put Lantern’s year-end balances into a classified balance sheet: decide what is current, split a loan into its current and noncurrent parts, and calculate working capital and the current ratio. Then look inside equity, at par value, additional paid-in capital, dividends and the statement of changes in equity.

segs.say: The balance sheet and equity. Put Lantern’s year-end balances into a classified balance sheet: decide what is current, split a loan into its current and noncurrent parts, and calculate working capital and the current ratio. Then look inside equity, at par value, additional paid-in capital, dividends and the statement of changes in equity.

scenes.head: You will be able to

segs.say: Classify assets and liabilities as current or noncurrent under US GAAP and IFRS, including the current portion of long-term debt.
Prepare a classified balance sheet in report form, with contra accounts shown on its face.
Calculate working capital and the current ratio, and the effect on them of debt classification and of when a dividend is paid.
Record the issue of par-value and no-par stock and the declaration and payment of a cash dividend.
Prepare a statement of changes in equity and reconcile it with the balance sheet.

scenes.head: In January Ana sends Lantern’s first annual statements to Coastline Bank and to the finance company that lent $20,000 for the van.

segs.say: In January Ana sends Lantern’s first annual statements to Coastline Bank and to the finance company that lent $20,000 for the van. Both lenders turn first to the balance sheet at 31 December 2026, and both ask the same questions. What must Lantern pay within the next year, and what will it have to pay it with? How much of the business is financed by its owner, and how much of that is profit Ana has left in the business rather than paid out?

scenes.head: The balance sheet answers those questions only if it is organised.

segs.say: The balance sheet answers those questions only if it is organised. A classified balance sheet groups assets and liabilities into current and noncurrent. A current asset is cash or an asset expected to be turned into cash, sold or used up within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer; a current liability is one expected to be settled within the same horizon. Everything else is a noncurrent asset or a noncurrent liability. The split lets a reader set what is due soon against what will be available soon, which is the first test of liquidity.

scenes.head: Within each group, US companies list assets in order of liquidity: cash first, then receivables, inventory and prepayments, then long-lived assets.

segs.say: Within each group, US companies list assets in order of liquidity: cash first, then receivables, inventory and prepayments, then long-lived assets. Liabilities follow in roughly the order they fall due, then equity. Long-term loans need care: most are repaid in instalments, so the part due within the next year is a current liability and the rest noncurrent, even though it is one loan. That part is the current portion of long-term debt, and Lantern’s van note is the example.

Lantern’s loan repayments on a time line from the balance sheet date (fictional). Only the van instalment due on 1 June 2027 falls before the one-year line, so only $5,000 of the $30,000 owed on the two notes is current.

scenes.head: The other half of the balance sheet is equity, the owners’ claim.

segs.say: The other half of the balance sheet is equity, the owners’ claim. It has two sources, and the balance sheet keeps them apart. Contributed capital is what owners paid in for their shares; retained earnings is the profit the business has earned and kept, net income since it began less every dividend. How contributed capital is split into par value and additional paid-in capital, how dividends are recorded, and how the statement of changes in equity ties the year together are the second half of this lesson.

scenes.head: Classification changes ratios, not totals

segs.say: Classification changes ratios, not totals. Moving the van’s next instalment from noncurrent to current liabilities leaves total liabilities and total assets unchanged. It changes working capital and the current ratio, and those are the numbers lenders write into their agreements. Classifying correctly is therefore not a matter of tidiness.

scenes.head: F01 introduced the test: an item is current if it will be realised, sold, used up or settled within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is…

segs.say: F01 introduced the test: an item is current if it will be realised, sold, used up or settled within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer. Three details matter when a balance sheet is prepared. Under US GAAP the operating cycle replaces the year only when it is longer than twelve months, and when there is no clearly defined cycle the one-year rule applies (ASC 210-10-45-3); Lantern, like most businesses, uses one year. Under IFRS, trade payables and accrued operating costs are current even if some are due after more than twelve months, because they belong to the operating cycle (IAS 1, paragraph 70). And a liability is current whenever the entity has no right, at the end of the reporting period, to defer its settlement for at least twelve months (IAS 1, paragraph 69(d), as amended from 2024; IFRS 18, which replaces IAS 1 for annual periods beginning on or after 1 January 2027, carries these requirements forward unchanged).

scenes.head: Some businesses, such as banks, have no clearly identifiable operating cycle, and IAS 1 lets them present assets and liabilities in order of…

segs.say: Some businesses, such as banks, have no clearly identifiable operating cycle, and IAS 1 lets them present assets and liabilities in order of liquidity without a current and noncurrent split when that is more relevant (paragraph 60). IAS 1 also doesn’t prescribe the order or format of the statement (paragraph 57), so some IFRS reporters list noncurrent assets first and show equity before liabilities. The facts are the same; only the layout differs.

scenes.head: Lantern’s classified balance sheet

segs.say: Lantern Coffee Co., Balance sheet at 31 December 2026

scenes.head: Current assets of $56,476 are dominated by cash ($42,940).

segs.say: Current assets of $56,476 are dominated by cash ($42,940). Receivables are shown at the gross $7,380 with the allowance of $584 deducted on the face of the statement, so the reader sees both what customers owe and what Lantern expects to collect. Prepaid insurance of $300 is the cover for January and February 2027, the last two months of the policy. Property and equipment appear at cost less accumulated depreciation, $12,000 − $2,000 and $30,000 − $2,800, for a net $37,200. Total assets are $93,676.

scenes.head: On the other side, current liabilities of $26,289 are the six items built up in the receivables and payables lesson.

segs.say: On the other side, current liabilities of $26,289 are the six items built up in the receivables and payables lesson. Noncurrent liabilities of $25,000 are notes payable: Coastline’s $10,000, due in one sum on 1 March 2028, fourteen months after the balance sheet date, and the $15,000 of the van note due after 31 December 2027. Equity is $42,387: $20,000 of common stock and $22,387 of retained earnings. Liabilities plus equity, 51,289 + 42,387, equal total assets of $93,676. The form shown, with assets above and liabilities and equity below, is the report form; the account form sets assets on the left and liabilities and equity on the right, like the two sides of an account.

chapters.title: The current portion of long-term debt

scenes.head: Lantern’s van note was $20,000, repayable in four yearly instalments of $5,000 from 1 June 2027.

segs.say: Lantern’s van note was $20,000, repayable in four yearly instalments of $5,000 from 1 June 2027. At 31 December 2026 the first instalment is due within twelve months and will be paid from current assets, so it is a current liability; the other $15,000 is not due until 2028 and later. The ledger keeps the note in one account, so at the year end the accountant moves the current part with a reclassification entry, adjustment e8. The entry changes no total and involves no cash: it moves $5,000 from one liability line to another.
Lantern’s reclassification at 31 December 2026 (e8, from the case)

scenes.head: The split is redone at every balance sheet date.

segs.say: The split is redone at every balance sheet date. By 31 December 2027 Lantern will have paid the first instalment, and two amounts will be due within the following year: the van’s second instalment on 1 June 2028 and the whole of Coastline’s note on 1 March 2028. The current portion will rise to 10,000 + 5,000 = 15,000 and only $10,000 of van instalments, those due in 2029 and 2030, will stay noncurrent. A loan that is comfortably long-term this year can become a large current liability next year just because time passes, which is why lenders and borrowers plan refinancing well before that happens.

scenes.head: Two complications are left to intermediate accounting.

segs.say: Two complications are left to intermediate accounting. If a borrower breaches a loan condition (a covenant) on or before the balance sheet date and the loan becomes repayable on demand, IFRS classifies the whole loan as current even if the lender agrees after the year end not to demand repayment (IAS 1, paragraph 74). And a short-term loan the company intends to refinance on long-term terms may in some circumstances be shown as noncurrent; US GAAP (ASC 470-10) and IFRS draw that line in different places.

chapters.title: Working capital and the current ratio

scenes.head: Two measures from F00 summarise the current section.

segs.say: Two measures from F00 summarise the current section. Working capital is current assets minus current liabilities; the current ratio divides one by the other. For Lantern, working capital is 56,476 − 26,289 = 30,187 and the current ratio is 56,476 ÷ 26,289 ≈ 2.15: about $2.15 of current assets for every dollar due within the year. Had the accountant forgotten e8, current liabilities would have been $21,289, working capital $35,187 and the ratio 2.65, a flattering picture of the same business.

scenes.head: The current ratio treats every current asset as equally able to pay bills, which is rarely true.

segs.say: The current ratio treats every current asset as equally able to pay bills, which is rarely true. Lantern’s cash alone, $42,940, exceeds all its current liabilities, while $6,100 of those liabilities will be settled by delivering events and coffee, not by paying cash. Judging whether 2.15 is comfortable for a coffee business, and comparing it with others, is the work of F03 Financial Statement Analysis; here the point is that the ratio is only as good as the classification behind it.

chapters.title: Contributed capital: par value and additional paid-in capital

scenes.head: A corporation’s charter states how many shares it may issue, its authorised shares, and for many companies a par value for each: a nominal amount…

segs.say: A corporation’s charter states how many shares it may issue, its authorised shares, and for many companies a par value for each: a nominal amount, often a cent or less, fixed by the charter and given meaning by state corporate law rather than by accounting standards. In Delaware, for example, shares with a par value may not be issued for less than par (Delaware General Corporation Law, section 153), and the capital a corporation records for them must be at least their total par value (section 154). Because par is usually tiny, it says nothing about what a share is worth.

scenes.head: When shares are issued, US practice splits the proceeds: Common Stock is credited with the par value of the shares issued, and the rest goes to…

segs.say: When shares are issued, US practice splits the proceeds: Common Stock is credited with the par value of the shares issued, and the rest goes to additional paid-in capital (APIC). No-par stock is credited in full to Common Stock, unless the board assigns it a stated value, which is then treated like par. Lantern’s shares have no par value, so all of Ana’s $20,000 went to Common Stock and its Additional Paid-in Capital account is empty. Had the same $20,000 bought 2,000 shares with a $1 par value, the entry would have split it: $2,000 to Common Stock and $18,000 to APIC. Total contributed capital is the same either way.
Ana’s investment as recorded (no-par shares, y1) and as it would have been recorded with a $1 par value (hypothetical)

scenes.head: Shares are sometimes issued for something other than cash, such as equipment or professional services.

segs.say: Shares are sometimes issued for something other than cash, such as equipment or professional services. The issue is then recorded at the fair value of the shares or of what is received, whichever can be measured more reliably, and split between par and APIC in the usual way.

scenes.head: The balance sheet or its notes give, for each class of stock, the par or stated value and the numbers of shares authorised, issued and outstanding.

segs.say: The balance sheet or its notes give, for each class of stock, the par or stated value and the numbers of shares authorised, issued and outstanding. Shares are issued when first sold. Some may later be bought back and held as treasury stock, shown as a deduction from equity; issued shares not held in treasury are the outstanding shares, the ones that vote and receive dividends. Some companies also issue preferred stock, which ranks ahead of common stock for dividends; F04 meets it as a source of fixed payments. Companies reporting under IFRS, and UK companies, usually call common stock share capital and APIC share premium.

scenes.head: A cash dividend involves three dates.

segs.say: A cash dividend involves three dates. On the declaration date the board votes the dividend, and it becomes a legal liability: debit Dividends (or Retained Earnings directly; Lantern uses a Dividends account, which is closed to Retained Earnings), credit dividends payable. The date of record fixes who will be paid, the shareholders on the register that day; no entry is made. On the payment date the company pays: debit Dividends Payable, credit Cash. Retained earnings fall when the dividend is declared, not when it is paid.

scenes.head: Lantern’s two dividends were declared and paid on the same day, $300 on 30 March and $4,700 on 15 December, so no dividend was owed at the year end.

segs.say: Lantern’s two dividends were declared and paid on the same day, $300 on 30 March and $4,700 on 15 December, so no dividend was owed at the year end. Suppose instead that the December dividend had been declared on 15 December and paid on 8 January 2027. Retained earnings and total equity would be exactly as reported, but the balance sheet would show $4,700 of dividends payable among current liabilities and $4,700 more cash. Working capital would not change (61,176 − 30,989 = 30,187), but the current ratio would fall from 2.15 to about 61,176 ÷ 30,989 ≈ 1.97, because the same amount has been added to both sides of a ratio above one.
If Lantern’s December dividend had been paid in January (hypothetical)

chapters.title: The statement of changes in equity

scenes.head: The statement of changes in equity explains how each component of equity moved from the start of the period to the end.

segs.say: The statement of changes in equity explains how each component of equity moved from the start of the period to the end. For Lantern’s first ten months it is short: common stock rose from nothing to $20,000 when Ana’s shares were issued, and retained earnings rose by net income of $27,387 and fell by dividends of $5,000, ending at $22,387. Each closing balance is the figure on the balance sheet, which is the articulation F01 introduced: net income from the income statement enters here, and total equity leaves here for the balance sheet.
Lantern Coffee Co., Statement of changes in equity for the ten months ended 31 December 2026
The same statement in columns, as companies usually present it (fictional)

scenes.head: Other components of equity

segs.say: Other components of equity. Larger companies’ statements have more columns. Additional paid-in capital and treasury stock each have their own. Under US GAAP so does accumulated other comprehensive income, which collects gains and losses that bypass net income, such as currency differences on foreign operations. IFRS reporters show similar amounts as reserves within equity, such as the revaluation surplus on property met in the long-lived assets lesson. The words vary too: statement of stockholders’ equity in much US practice, statement of changes in equity under IFRS.

scenes.head: Working capital

segs.say: Working capital: Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities.
Current assets: Cash and assets expected to become cash, be sold or be used up within one year or the operating cycle ($).
Current liabilities: Obligations due within the same horizon, including the current portion of long-term debt ($).

scenes.head: Current ratio

segs.say: Current ratio: Current ratio = (Current assets)/(Current liabilities).
Current assets: As above ($).
Current liabilities: As above; must be greater than zero ($).
Lantern: 56,476 ÷ 26,289 ≈ 2.15. A pure number.

scenes.head: Splitting a loan at the balance sheet date

segs.say: Splitting a loan at the balance sheet date: Noncurrent portion = Principal outstanding − Principal due within 12 months.
Principal outstanding: Loan principal owed at the balance sheet date ($).
Principal due within 12 months: Instalments due in the next year: the current portion of long-term debt ($).
Interest accrued to the balance sheet date is a separate current liability (Interest Payable).

scenes.head: Common stock and additional paid-in capital on an issue of shares

segs.say: Common stock and additional paid-in capital on an issue of shares: Common stock = N × Par, APIC = N × (P − Par).
N: Number of shares issued (shares).
P: Issue price per share ($ per share).
Par: Par (or stated) value per share; for no-par stock without a stated value, all proceeds go to common stock ($ per share).

scenes.head: Cash dividend declared

segs.say: Cash dividend declared: Dividend = d × Nₒᵤₜ.
d: Dividend per share declared by the board ($ per share).
Nₒᵤₜ: Shares outstanding (issued shares less treasury shares) on the date of record (shares).

scenes.head: Largest cash payment that keeps a minimum current ratio

segs.say: Largest cash payment that keeps a minimum current ratio: Maximum payment = CA − k × CL.
CA, CL: Current assets and current liabilities before the payment ($).
k: Minimum current ratio required, for example by a loan agreement.
It assumes this: The payment is made in cash from current assets and settles nothing in current liabilities (for example, a dividend paid at once).
If the dividend is declared but not yet paid, it adds to current liabilities instead, and the limit is CA ÷ k − CL.

chapters.title: Example: A florist’s classified balance sheet

scenes.head: A florist’s classified balance sheet

segs.say: Thistle Lane Florists, a fictional shop, has these balances at 31 December 2026: Cash $8,400; Accounts Receivable $6,200; Allowance for Doubtful Accounts $300; Inventory (flowers and pots) $3,100; Prepaid Rent for January–March $1,800; Van $36,000; Accumulated Depreciation—Van $9,000; Accounts Payable $4,900; Wages Payable $1,100; Unearned Revenue (wedding deposits for spring) $2,600; Interest Payable $450; a bank loan of $18,000 repayable at $6,000 each 1 July; Common Stock $10,000. Find current assets, current liabilities, working capital, the current ratio and retained earnings.

scenes.head: A florist’s classified balance sheet

segs.say: Step 1. Current assets, with the allowance deducted: 8,400 + 6,200 − 300 + 3,100 + 1,800 = 19,200. Prepaid rent is current: it will be used up within the year.
Step 2. Split the loan: the $6,000 due on 1 July 2027 is current; 18,000 − 6,000 = 12,000 is noncurrent. Current liabilities: 4,900 + 1,100 + 2,600 + 450 + 6,000 = 15,050.
Step 3. Working capital 19,200 − 15,050 = 4,150; current ratio 19,200 ÷ 15,050 ≈ 1.28.

scenes.head: A florist’s classified balance sheet

segs.say: Current assets $19,200; current liabilities $15,050 (including the $6,000 current portion of the loan); working capital $4,150; current ratio about 1.28; retained earnings $9,150.
Without the split the florist would have shown current liabilities of $9,050 and a ratio of about 2.12, hiding the fact that a July loan payment will take most of its cash.

chapters.title: Example: A furniture maker’s year in equity

scenes.head: A furniture maker’s year in equity

segs.say: Hazelmere Furniture Inc., a fictional company, has 1,000,000 shares of $0.01 par value common stock authorised. On 1 January 2026 it has 40,000 shares issued and outstanding, with Common Stock $400, Additional Paid-in Capital $239,600 and Retained Earnings $85,000. On 1 June it issues 10,000 more shares at $15 each for cash. Net income for 2026 is $64,000, and on 10 December the board declares a dividend of $0.40 a share to shareholders of record on 31 December, payable on 15 January 2027. Record the share issue and the dividend, and prepare the statement of changes in equity.

scenes.head: A furniture maker’s year in equity

segs.say: Step 2. Shares outstanding at the date of record: 40,000 + 10,000 = 50,000. Dividend 0.40 × 50,000 = 20,000, recorded on 10 December as a liability.
Step 3. Retained earnings: 85,000 + 64,000 − 20,000 = 129,000. The dividend reduces 2026’s retained earnings although the cash leaves in 2027.

Step 4. Closing equity: 500 + 389,500 + 129,000 = 519,000, which agrees with 325,000 + 150,000 + 64,000 − 20,000. The $20,000 of dividends payable appears among current liabilities on the balance sheet.

scenes.head: A furniture maker’s year in equity

segs.say: Debit Cash 150,000; credit Common Stock 100 and APIC 149,900. Debit Dividends 20,000; credit Dividends Payable 20,000 (paid in January). Equity at 31 December 2026: Common Stock $500, APIC $389,500, Retained Earnings $129,000, total $519,000.

Almost all of the $390,000 Hazelmere’s shareholders have paid in sits in APIC, because the par value is a cent. A reader judging how much capital the owners put in should add Common Stock and APIC together; the split between them is a legal formality.

chapters.title: Example: How much more can Lantern pay Ana?

scenes.head: How much more can Lantern pay Ana?

segs.say: Suppose the van’s finance agreement requires Lantern to keep a current ratio of at least 1.5 at each year end, and that on 31 December 2026 Ana is considering an extra dividend of $15,000 on top of the $5,000 already paid. Using the balance sheet (current assets $56,476, current liabilities $26,289, retained earnings $22,387), test the dividend paid on 31 December and the same dividend declared on 31 December but paid in January, and find the largest dividend each way.

scenes.head: How much more can Lantern pay Ana?

segs.say: Step 1. Paid at once: current assets fall to 56,476 − 15,000 = 41,476; current liabilities stay at 26,289; ratio 41,476 ÷ 26,289 ≈ 1.58. The test is passed.
Step 2. Declared, paid in January: current liabilities rise to 26,289 + 15,000 = 41,289; current assets stay at 56,476; ratio 56,476 ÷ 41,289 ≈ 1.37. The test is failed.
Step 3. Largest dividend paid at once (ratio-headroom formula): 56,476 − 1.5 × 26,289 = 17,042.50. Largest declared but unpaid: 56,476 ÷ 1.5 − 26,289 ≈ 11,361.67.

Step 4. Either way working capital falls by 15,000, to 30,187 − 15,000 = 15,187, and retained earnings to 22,387 − 15,000 = 7,387. Cash after paying it would be 42,940 − 15,000 = 27,940, against $20,189 of current liabilities that need cash in the next five months.

scenes.head: How much more can Lantern pay Ana?

segs.say: A $15,000 dividend paid on 31 December keeps the ratio at about 1.58; declared then and paid in January it would push the ratio to about 1.37 and breach a 1.5 minimum. The limits are about $17,043 paid at once and about $11,362 declared but unpaid.

The same dividend can pass or fail a ratio test depending on when it is paid, because a payable adds to the denominator while a payment subtracts from the numerator. A prudent answer for Ana is smaller still: the business needs cash for January’s bills, the June instalment and the tax payment, and a lender reads the whole balance sheet, not just one ratio.

scenes.head: Lantern’s working capital and current ratio at 31 December 2026

segs.say: Start from Lantern’s balance sheet. Change how much of the long-term debt is classified as current (the default, $5,000, is adjustment e8), and add a dividend paid in cash or declared but unpaid. Watch working capital and the current ratio, and how much room is left under a minimum ratio. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: An interactive

segs.say: Build Lantern’s statement of changes in equity and balance sheet from its year: place each account on the right statement, then work out ending retained earnings and total assets. Contra accounts go with the assets they reduce. Pause the video and try it in the Explore section of this lesson.

scenes.head: “A long-term loan is a noncurrent liability.”

segs.say: “A long-term loan is a noncurrent liability.”. Only the part not due within the next year is noncurrent. Instalments due in the next twelve months are current, and a loan repayable in one sum becomes wholly current a year before it falls due: Coastline’s note will be current at 31 December 2027.

scenes.head: “Reclassifying the current portion means paying it.”

segs.say: “Reclassifying the current portion means paying it.”. Entry e8 moves $5,000 from Notes Payable to Current Portion of Long-Term Debt. No cash moves, and total liabilities don’t change; the payment is recorded on 1 June 2027.

scenes.head: “Par value is what a share is worth.”

segs.say: “Par value is what a share is worth.”. In states such as Delaware, par is a legal minimum issue price, usually a cent or less. Hazelmere’s shares sold at $15 with a par of $0.01; the other $14.99 is additional paid-in capital. Market value, book value and par are three different numbers.

scenes.head: “Dividends reduce retained earnings when they are paid.”

segs.say: “Dividends reduce retained earnings when they are paid.”. Retained earnings fall on the declaration date, when the dividend becomes a liability. The payment settles Dividends Payable and doesn’t touch equity. No entry is made on the date of record.

scenes.head: “Accumulated depreciation and the allowance are liabilities because they have credit balances.”

segs.say: “Accumulated depreciation and the allowance are liabilities because they have credit balances.”. Both are contra-assets. They are deducted from the assets they belong to, on the face of the balance sheet or in a note. Listing them as liabilities would overstate both total assets and total liabilities.

scenes.head: Lenders read the classified balance sheet as the starting point for their own tests.

segs.say: Lenders read the classified balance sheet as the starting point for their own tests. Coastline’s loan officer checks that current liabilities include everything due within the year, including the van instalment and the tax, and that the current assets are what they claim to be: cash confirmed by the bank, receivables net of a supported allowance, inventory written down where needed. Loan agreements often set a minimum current ratio or working capital, and a breach can make a loan repayable on demand, which would itself turn a noncurrent liability into a current one. The applied example shows how much the timing of a single payment can matter.

scenes.head: Equity is read for what it says about the owners’ commitment.

segs.say: Equity is read for what it says about the owners’ commitment. Lantern’s $20,000 of common stock is Ana’s investment; its $22,387 of retained earnings is profit she has left in the business, more than four times the $5,000 paid out. A lender likes that: retained earnings are a cushion that absorbs losses before the lender is affected. When Lantern takes on an outside investor, as the F00 scenario imagines, the statement of changes in equity will record the new shares, and the par and APIC split will depend on the charter.

scenes.head: For Ana the balance sheet is also a planning tool.

segs.say: For Ana the balance sheet is also a planning tool. It shows $42,940 of cash, but $20,189 of it is already spoken for by liabilities due in the next five months, and the first van instalment and the tax payment fall in the same weeks of the year. Before buying a new machine or paying a larger dividend she should prepare a cash budget for 2027, starting from this balance sheet. The statement of cash flows, the subject of the next module, explains how the year’s cash came to be $42,940 in the first place.

scenes.head: What to remember

segs.say: A classified balance sheet separates current items (within one year, or the operating cycle if longer) from noncurrent ones; US companies list assets in order of liquidity and IFRS doesn’t prescribe an order.
IFRS classifies a liability as current if it is due within twelve months or the entity has no right at the period end to defer settlement for twelve months (IAS 1, carried into IFRS 18 from 2027).
The current portion of long-term debt is the principal due within the next year; Lantern’s e8 moves $5,000 of the van note to current, leaving $25,000 of notes payable noncurrent.
Lantern’s balance sheet: total assets $93,676 = liabilities $51,289 + equity $42,387; working capital $30,187; current ratio about 2.15 (2.65 if e8 were forgotten).
Contributed capital is split between common stock (par or stated value) and additional paid-in capital; no-par stock without a stated value goes wholly to common stock, as Lantern’s $20,000 did.
A cash dividend reduces retained earnings on the declaration date and creates dividends payable; the date of record needs no entry; payment settles the liability.
The statement of changes in equity reconciles each component: Lantern’s retained earnings go from 0 + 27,387 − 5,000 to $22,387, and total equity to $42,387, the balance sheet figure.
